title: Impact of organizational factors on adherence to laboratory testing protocols in adult HIV care in Lusaka, Zambia
venue: Carolina Digital Repository (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous operational research studies have demonstrated the feasibility of large-scale public sector ART programs in resource-limited settings. However, organizational and structural determinants of quality of care have not been studied. METHODS: We estimate multivariate regression models using data from 13 urban HIV treatment facilities in Zambia to assess the impact of structural determinants on health workers' adherence to national guidelines for conducting laboratory tests such as CD4, hemoglobin and liver function and WHO staging during initial and follow-up visits as part of Zambian HIV care and treatment program. RESULTS: CD4 tests were more routinely ordered during initial history and physical (IHP) than follow-up (FUP) visits (93.0 % vs. 85.5 %; p < 0.01). More physical space, higher staff turnover and greater facility experience with ART was associated with greater odds of conducting tests. Higher staff experience decreased the odds of conducting CD4 tests in FUP (OR 0.93; p < 0.05) and WHO staging in IHP visit (OR 0.90; p < 0.05) but increased the odds of conducting hemoglobin test in IHP visit (OR 1.05; p < 0.05). Higher staff burnout increased the odds of conducting CD4 test during FUP (OR 1.14; p < 0.05) but decreased the odds of conducting hemoglobin test in IHP visit (0.77; p < 0.05) and CD4 test in IHP visit (OR 0.78; p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: Physical space plays an important role in ensuring high quality care in resource-limited setting. In the context of protocolized care, new staff members are likely to be more diligent in following the protocol verbatim rather than relying on memory and experience thereby improving adherence. Future studies should use prospective data to confirm the findings reported here.

summary.oneLiner: In 13 Lusaka HIV clinics, staff and facility factors such as physical space and staff burnout showed mixed associations with following lab-testing protocols.
summary.overview: The study looked at 13 urban HIV clinics in Lusaka, Zambia, to see whether how the organization is set up, such as space, staffing, burnout and staff experience, relates to whether health workers order required lab tests like CD4 counts and hemoglobin. Using 2007 patient visit records and a staff survey, the authors ran multilevel regressions, a statistical method that accounts for patients being grouped within facilities. Physical space and staff turnover were linked to higher odds of ordering tests, while staff experience and burnout had mixed, sometimes counterintuitive, links depending on the test and visit type. The authors stress these are associations from one year of data in one city, not proven causes, and they call for prospective studies to confirm them.
summary.question: Do organizational and structural factors, such as physical space, staffing levels, staff burnout, absenteeism, experience and turnover, relate to how well health workers adhere to national guidelines for laboratory tests during initial and follow-up HIV care visits?
summary.method: Multi-level logistic regression models (a statistical method for visit-level yes/no outcomes that accounts for visits being grouped within facility-months), with facility-month as the grouping level and predictors as fixed effects. Two nested model variants were tested, and the authors report the second, which adds absenteeism and burnout, because those coefficients were significant.
summary.data: Electronic medical records from the SmartCare database for adult patients (16 or older) with HIV who were enrolled in care during calendar year 2007, covering 13 urban HIV treatment facilities in Lusaka Urban District. Staff burnout, experience, absenteeism and turnover came from a 2007 healthcare worker survey with roughly 500 anonymous responses. Physical space came from facility architectural plans, and staffing ratios from overtime payment records.
findings: CD4 tests were more routinely ordered at initial history and physical (IHP) visits than at follow-up (FUP) visits (93.0% vs. 85.5%; p < 0.01), per the abstract; the results section reports 85.4% of IHP visits with CD4 results within 4 weeks.
More physical space, higher staff turnover and greater facility experience with ART were associated with greater odds of conducting tests.

Higher staff experience was associated with lower odds of CD4 tests at follow-up (OR 0.93) and WHO staging at initial visits (OR 0.90), but higher odds of hemoglobin tests at initial visits (OR 1.05).
Higher staff burnout was associated with higher odds of CD4 tests at follow-up (OR 1.14) but lower odds of hemoglobin tests (OR 0.77) and CD4 tests (OR 0.78) at initial visits.
The authors suggest that physical space plays an important role in quality of care in resource-limited settings, and that new staff may follow protocols more closely, which could improve adherence.

The authors note limited variation in some predictors and very few stage IV patients, which may have reduced statistical power to detect effects, and they say the results cannot be used to judge absolute quality of care.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that space, staffing and turnover patterns may matter for protocol adherence in busy, protocolized HIV programs, and that turnover could be beneficial if it replaces demotivated or burnt-out staff. They also say their results challenge some established relationships between workload, burnout and experience and appropriate care, and that prospective data are needed before policy conclusions are drawn. The paper does not give specific recommendations to managers or investors.
